findings.evidence:
Since an e-mail address identifies exactly one person, the job groups
customers by lower-cased e-mail, keeps the oldest record of each group,
moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The design's Context states the opposite: "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." As written, the first nightly run fuses those distinct buyers into the oldest record, moves every buyer's orders under one name and billing address, and deletes the other buyers' records. Pick a merge key that actually identifies one person (e.g. e-mail plus name and billing address, or restrict to guest-created records), or exclude shared mailboxes, and state the evidence that the chosen key is unique per person. Then add the matching spec scenario ("two buyers share a mailbox → both records remain").
findings.title: The merge key rests on an assumption the design's own context refutes

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The job deletes customer rows (with their name and billing address) and rewrites `orders.customer_id`; nothing in the plan keeps the original rows or the order-to-customer mapping, so a wrong merge cannot be undone. Add a way back — record each merge (merged id → kept id, original row, moved order ids) before deleting, or soft-delete — and a staged rollout such as a dry-run report reviewed before the first destructive run. Add a task and a scenario for it.
findings.title: Deleting merged records is irreversible, with no way back

findings.evidence: - **THEN** one record remains, holding the orders of both
findings.recommendation: The requirement does not say what happens when the merged records differ in name or billing address (whose values survive, or whether they are merged at all), nor how e-mails that differ only in case are treated — the design lower-cases them, the spec only says "share an e-mail address". Add scenarios for case-variant e-mails, for records with conflicting name/billing address, and for a shared business mailbox (see R-skeptic-1), and extend task 1.1 with the tests that verify them.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path and leaves the surviving data undefined

findings.recommendation: The proposal adds "A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address." — something to schedule, run and monitor — yet `operations` is unticked with no reason, and Impact lists only `jobs/merge_customers.py` with no scheduler entry. Tick `operations` so its expert reviews how the job is scheduled, observed and stopped, or give the reason on its line.
findings.title: A new scheduled job with the operations domain unticked
